what_the_text_says: An inventory of relationships may be useful; a large bank may map parts of a relationship to business units. A bank may choose not to keep extensive inventories of limited-risk relationships.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: Inventory flag for AI-enabled services and the upstream model provider behind each one.
note: The text names the inventory, not AI services or upstream providers.

what_the_text_says: Identify the most salient risks with subject-matter experts. A bank is not expected to identify every possible risk.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: A short list of AI-specific risks per vendor: wrong output, a silent change of model, use of bank data.

what_the_text_says: Weigh the magnitude of harm and its likelihood. Higher-risk relationships could include those that, if disrupted, attacked or in breach of contract terms, could cause a non-trivial violation of law, material harm to financial condition or a significant disruption, where that is materially likely.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: Impact if a wrong output reaches a customer, and the share of activity that depends on it.
note: The log's material flag, 4 hours or more of customer impact, is my threshold for a significant disruption; the text sets none.

what_the_text_says: Core processing providers are likely to be assessed as higher risk by most banks (B.1.iii). The Overview lists services central to operations: core processing, cloud processing, cloud storage, compliance tools, and fintech partners. A core processor serving a limited part of the business may be lower risk.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: Service type and share of activity.
note: Used as the text-examples rule in step 2. The cloud, compliance and fintech types are my choice to tier HIGH, not the text's, and the 30 percent share line is mine.

what_the_text_says: The agencies ask whether a list of characteristics that generally indicate high risk would help, and which to include.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: Dependence on one upstream model provider; no notice before a model change; training on or long retention of bank data.
note: No AI term appears in the text. These are the candidate characteristics tested here.

what_the_text_says: May cover financial condition, key personnel, staffing and qualifications, legal and regulatory compliance, insurance, and information security and cybersecurity, and the effectiveness of risk management practices.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: SOC report (my choice for information security), insurance, financial condition and key personnel.
note: Used as the questionnaire in step 1.

what_the_text_says: Depth of due diligence depends on risk. The text does not list evidence of model performance, version history or data-use terms.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: Performance evidence on the bank's own slices; model version log; terms on use of bank data for training.

what_the_text_says: No generally applicable expected terms. May address service levels, confidentiality and information security, subcontractors, operational resilience and termination. A bank may ask for activity-specific addenda.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: An addendum covering notice before a model change, training use, retention period and audit rights over upstream use.
note: The text's room for activity-specific addenda fits this; a model-change notice is not named.

what_the_text_says: Examples include reviewing updated due diligence and performance reports, and periodic testing of the bank's controls and, in certain circumstances, of the third party's services; also customer complaints.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: Re-run a fixed evaluation set against the vendor's output on a schedule; review the vendor's model version log.
note: Testing the third party's services is the closest named example.

what_the_text_says: Subcontractors can heighten risk. Oversight may use contract terms on their use, or an assessment of the third party's own third-party risk management. The bank stays responsible.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: Treat the upstream model provider as a subcontractor: name it in the contract and require notice of change.
note: The text does not say that an upstream model provider is a subcontractor.

what_the_text_says: Banks commonly consider the overall relationship where they are exposed to concentration risk from relying on one third party for extensive services.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: Share of the bank's AI-enabled activity that sits on one upstream provider across several vendors.
note: Concentration inside one third party is covered; several vendors sharing one provider is not mentioned.

what_the_text_says: Resilience plans, alternative backup providers and data backed up at a separate site may help for higher-risk relationships.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: A tested fallback when the model is unavailable (rules or a person), and the time to switch to a second provider.

what_the_text_says: Costs and fees, transition time, disruption and data retention and destruction are factors a bank may weigh when deciding whether to terminate; advanced planning may help.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: Deletion of bank data at the vendor and at its upstream model provider, including logs and tuned copies.

what_the_text_says: Some residual risk is unavoidable. Acceptance follows the bank's risk appetite, and limited bargaining power may restrict what a bank can do.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: Written acceptance of a known gap, for example a vendor that gives no change notice.

what_the_text_says: Clear roles, risk appetite and tolerances, reporting to senior management and the board, documentation and periodic independent review.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: A named owner for model-change review; AI-enabled vendors in board reporting.

what_the_text_says: Relying on third-party technology to help oversee third parties can itself involve risks.
evidence_for_an_ai_enabled_vendor: If an AI tool summarizes vendor documents, treat that tool as a third party too.
